notes: Moncton publishes one document with English and French side by side on every line. The risk this file exists to catch is language bleed: an English question retrieving a chunk that is half French, or a clause whose text interleaves the two ('158 No development shall be permitted and no main 158 Les aménagements ne sont permis et les').
expect_text therefore pins English sentences that sit directly beside their French translation in the source. If the gutter split regresses, the clause text will carry French and these fail.
Definitions are cited under section 1 with the defined term as the heading. Moncton numbers none of them, so a positional number would cite a provision that does not exist.

questions.question: What is a garden suite?
questions.why: Definitions are unbolded and quoted in this bylaw, so the bold gate blocked every one of them until quotes were treated as the marker.

questions.question: Can I put a granny flat in my back yard for my mother?
questions.why: The bylaw never says 'granny flat'. Only semantic retrieval bridges this.

questions.question: How many garden suites can I have on one lot?
expect_text: No more than one garden suite
questions.why: A numbered provision with no inline title. Read as titled, its first line became a truncated heading and the text began mid-sentence.

questions.question: Can I keep chickens in my back yard?
questions.why: Urban agriculture. expect_text pins the coop standards, which sat on a page whose French column had to be separated out.

questions.question: Am I allowed to slaughter hens on my property?
questions.why: A short provision whose French translation sits on the same line; language bleed shows up here first.

questions.question: What is the minimum lot area for a semi-detached dwelling?
questions.why: A full-width bilingual table. Splitting it at the gutter would have severed each zone column from its values, so the table is deliberately kept whole and cited by its caption.
